summary: Defines how IPv6 packets are carried over PPP links, including the control protocol that sets up IPv6 and how link-local addresses are formed. It replaces RFC 2023. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 5072 and RFC 5172.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is like a direct line between two computers. This explains how to use that line for IPv6 and how each end gets its local address.

questions: how does ipv6 work over ppp
how is the ppp interface identifier negotiated
what is the ppp protocol number for ipv6
subtitle: How IPv6 packets travel over PPP links, and how the two ends agree on an interface identifier.

tldr.problem: PPP can carry many network-layer protocols, but each one needs a way to be set up and configured on the link. IPv6 also needs each end of the link to get an address component that is unique.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2472 defines the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP), which reuses the LCP packet exchange, and two options: one to negotiate a 64-bit interface identifier and one to negotiate IPv6 compression. It also says how to form link-local addresses from the identifier.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 2023 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5072 and RFC 5172.

today: RFC 2472 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 5072 and RFC 5172, so those are the current definitions. It replaced RFC 2023.

sections.title: PPP and the Role of IPV6CP
sections.content:
PPP has three main components: a method for encapsulating datagrams over serial links, a Link Control Protocol (LCP) for establishing, configuring and testing the data-link connection, and a family of Network Control Protocols (NCPs) for configuring network-layer protocols. Each end first sends LCP packets to bring up the link. Then it sends NCP packets to choose and configure one or more network-layer protocols.

In this document the NCP for IPv6 is called the IPv6 Control Protocol (IPV6CP). The link stays configured until explicit LCP or NCP packets close it, or until an external event such as a power failure or carrier drop occurs.
sections.plainLanguage: Two computers first agree how to use the wire at all. Then they agree which languages to speak on it. IPV6CP is the part where they agree to speak IPv6.

sections.title: Sending IPv6 Datagrams
sections.content:
Before any IPv6 packet is sent, PPP MUST reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and IPV6CP MUST reach the Opened state. Exactly one IPv6 packet is placed in the Information field of each PPP frame, and the frame's Protocol field is hex 0057 (Internet Protocol Version 6).

The maximum length of an IPv6 packet on a PPP link equals the maximum length of the Information field of a PPP frame. PPP links supporting IPv6 MUST allow an Information field at least as large as the minimum link MTU that IPv6 requires.
sections.plainLanguage: Each PPP envelope holds exactly one IPv6 packet, and the envelope is stamped with a special code so the receiver knows it is IPv6. The envelope must be big enough for the smallest packet IPv6 allows.

sections.title: How IPV6CP Works
sections.content:
IPV6CP is configuring, enabling and disabling the IPv6 modules on both ends of the link. It is exactly the same as LCP, with a few exceptions. IPV6CP packets are carried in PPP frames whose Protocol field is hex 8057 (IPv6 Control Protocol), one packet per frame.

Only Codes 1 through 7 are used: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject. Other Codes are treated as unrecognized and should produce a Code-Reject.

IPV6CP packets received before the Network-Layer Protocol phase should be silently discarded. An implementation should be ready to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before it times out waiting for a Configure-Ack. The RFC suggests giving up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.
sections.plainLanguage: IPV6CP uses the same polite back-and-forth as the first conversation: ask, accept, suggest something else, or refuse. It just uses its own stamp on the envelope and a shorter list of message types.

sections.title: Configuration Options
sections.content:
IPV6CP uses the LCP option format with its own set of options. If an option is missing from a Configure-Request, its default value is assumed. Two options are defined: type 1, Interface-Identifier, and type 2, IPv6-Compression-Protocol. Any further options are to be defined in separate documents.

Interface-Identifier negotiates a 64-bit identifier for the local end, used for address autoconfiguration. A Configure-Request MUST contain exactly one instance of the option, and after negotiation the two ends MUST have different values. By default an implementation SHOULD attempt to negotiate it.

IPv6-Compression-Protocol negotiates a specific IPv6 packet compression protocol, and indicates the ability to receive compressed packets. Each end must request it separately for compression in both directions. By default compression is not enabled, and the RFC says no field values are currently assigned. It is separate from compression negotiated through the Compression Control Protocol (CCP).
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends can settle on two things: a name tag for each side that nobody else on the line shares, and whether to squash IPv6 packets to make them smaller. Squashing is off unless both ask for it.

sections.title: Negotiating the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
Before asking, an implementation picks a tentative identifier. In preference order: build it from an IEEE EUI-48 or EUI-64 identifier if one exists anywhere on the node; otherwise use another source of uniqueness such as link-layer addresses or machine serial numbers; otherwise generate a random number. The identifier should be non-zero and, if possible, reproducible across restarts, so that global addresses formed from it stay stable. When derived from an EUI-64, the only change is inverting the u (universal/local) bit. An EUI-48 is first converted to EUI-64 by inserting 0xFF and 0xFE in the middle. In the other two methods the u bit MUST be zero.

When a peer receives a Configure-Request carrying the option, it compares the value with the one in its own last Configure-Request:

  • Different and received value is zero: send a Configure-Nak suggesting a different non-zero value.
  • Different and received value is non-zero: send a Configure-Ack.
  • Equal and non-zero: send a Configure-Nak suggesting a different non-zero value.
  • Both zero: terminate the negotiation with a Configure-Reject, since no unique identifier can be negotiated.

If a peer does not implement the option, it sends a Configure-Rej. If no valid identifier is agreed, no default is assumed, and recovery is unspecified; one approach is manual configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side picks a name tag, ideally one built from its network card's built-in number. If both pick the same tag, one side suggests a different one. If neither can think of a good tag, they give up and a person has to set one by hand.

sections.title: Autoconfiguration and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
The interface identifier of a PPP interface's IPv6 unicast addresses SHOULD be negotiated during IPV6CP. Because the identifier is negotiated to be unique on the link, duplicate address detection in stateless autoconfiguration is redundant. The RFC therefore recommends that, for PPP links with the Interface-Identifier option enabled, the default of the DupAddrDetectTransmits variable be zero.

A link-local address on a PPP interface is 10 bits of 1111111010 (the prefix FE80::), then 54 zero bits, then the 64-bit interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Once each side has its own unique name tag, nobody needs to double-check that the tag is taken. The local address is just a fixed beginning followed by that name tag.
